"Small fry" refers to a person — or a group of people — who are unimportant, low in power, or of little significance, especially when compared to those who hold real authority, influence, or status.

Think of a corporate ladder. At the top sit the CEO, the board members, the decision-makers. At the bottom are the entry-level workers with little power over anything. Those at the bottom? They are the small fry. The word captures the idea of someone who barely registers on the scale of importance — someone whose actions, decisions, or presence don't carry much weight in the larger picture.

A person is called small fry when they lack one or more of the following:

  • Power — they can't make significant decisions or affect outcomes
  • Influence — people don't listen to them or change their behaviour because of them
  • Status — they are low in rank, hierarchy, or social standing
  • Resources — they may be financially minor or operationally insignificant
  • Threat level — they don't pose a serious danger or challenge to anyone powerful

The term is almost always relative. Someone might be small fry compared to a billionaire, but significant in their own neighbourhood. Context determines the comparison.

Less commonly, "small fry" is also used as a warm, informal way to refer to young children — the small, little ones. In this sense, it's not dismissive at all; it's almost affectionate.

"The event is designed for the small fry — games, balloons, and cartoons."

However, this usage is far less frequent in modern English. The dominant meaning is the one about unimportant or powerless people.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

When used about adults and their importance, "small fry" carries a tone that is usually dismissive or belittling. It signals that the speaker does not consider the person worth serious attention or concern. Sometimes it is said with contempt; other times it is a neutral, matter-of-fact assessment.

Importantly, "small fry" is not always an insult directed at someone. It can be used to describe someone's position objectively, or even said by people about themselves with humility.

"We're just small fry compared to those multinational companies."

Here the speaker is simply acknowledging their own limited scale — not ashamed, just realistic.
Grammar: Singular and Plural Are the Same

This is an important detail. "Small fry" does not change its form whether you are talking about one person or many.

  • One person → "He is small fry." ✅
  • Many people → "They are small fry." ✅

You would not say "small fries" when talking about unimportant people. The plural form does not change. (Note: "small fries" only works when you're literally talking about french fries — the food.)
Where You'll See This Word Used

"Small fry" appears most naturally in contexts where there are clear hierarchies of power, money, or authority:

Crime and law enforcement:

"The detective wasn't interested in arresting small fry. She wanted to catch the man at the top of the entire smuggling operation."

Here, the foot soldiers or minor criminals are small fry. The mastermind is the real target.

Business and finance:

"Our startup is small fry in the global technology market, but we're growing fast."

A small company, with little market share or influence, is small fry next to the giants.

Politics and power:

"The minister ignored the complaints. The protestors were small fry — no votes, no money, no connections."

The protestors lacked the levers of power, so they were dismissed.

Everyday comparisons:

"Don't worry about competing with him. He's small fry — he has no real clients or reputation yet."

To fully understand what small fry means, it helps to know what the opposite looks like. The contrasting idea is captured by phrases like:

  • "Big fish" — a powerful, important person
  • "The big players" — dominant forces in a field
  • "The heavyweights" — people with serious influence
  • "The top brass" — high-ranking officials or leaders

Small fry exist in relation to these bigger forces. Without the contrast, the term loses some of its meaning.

What it meansUnimportant or low-power person/group (also informally: young children)
ToneDismissive, belittling, or simply realistic — depending on context
Singular/pluralSame form — "small fry" for both one and many
Opposite ideaBig fish, the top brass, the major players

If you ever hear or read "small fry," ask yourself: small compared to whom, and in what world? The word always implies a bigger pond with bigger fish swimming in it. The small fry are the ones at the bottom — overlooked, underestimated, and relatively powerless. Whether that is said with contempt, with pity, or with simple honesty depends entirely on who is saying it and why.
